years, this repository was one of the most useful public places for Dota 2 players to report gameplay issues, document bugs, and communicate problems in a way that could realistically be seen by Valve developers. It served as a direct and practical channel between the player community and the people maintaining the game. Unfortunately, over the last few months, that value has been seriously damaged by the constant activity pattern of a specific user: @Dota-Explorer. I am naming the account only so Valve and/or GitHub staff can review the issue history, blocking behavior, duplicates, reposting patterns, and overall impact on the repository. This report is not about targeting a person for having opinions or for reporting bugs frequently. The concern is about repeated disruptive behavior that is making the issue tracker significantly less useful for everyone. I myself, as well as other notable community members, such as @Leamare or @sikleq, were harassed and blindly accused by this user multiple times - both on- and off- GitHub. ## Reference to GitHub Acceptable Use Policies I believe this situation should be reviewed in the context of GitHub’s Acceptable Use Policies: https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/acceptable-use-policies/github-acceptable-use-policies In particular, GitHub states that collaboration only works when users are able to work together in good faith. The policies also mention that GitHub does not allow activity that is off-topic or interacts with platform features in a way that significantly or repeatedly disrupts the experience of other users. This report is not intended to claim that a violation has already been definitively proven. Rather, I am asking Valve and community contributors to review whether the repeated issue flooding, reposting of closed topics, and blocking of community discussion may fall under disruptive use of GitHub Issues, spam-like behavior, or misuse of platform features. ## Main Concern The problem is not simply that this user posts a lot. High activity by itself is not necessarily harmful if the reports are accurate, useful, and open to normal discussion. The issue is that the repository is being flooded with an excessive number of issues every single day, many of which appear to be duplicates, misleading, unverifiable, based on personal accusations, or not actual gameplay bugs. This volume of posts makes it much harder for legitimate reports to be noticed. Important bugs and useful technical issues are quickly pushed down or buried under a constant stream of low-quality issues. For example, real WebAPI issues have already been reported and then quickly piled up under unrelated or lower-quality reports. In-game Economics bugs also become much harder to notice, even though those can have real impact on players, items, rewards, purchases, and the overall game experience. This is especially damaging because Dota 2 has many different categories of issues that require attention: gameplay bugs, server problems, WebAPI issues, item/economy bugs, UI problems, matchmaking issues, cosmetics, replays, tooltips, and more. When one user dominates the issue tracker with constant posts, the whole reporting system becomes harder to use. Important issues from other users become less visible, harder to search for, and less likely to receive discussion or confirmation. ## Reposting and Artificial Visibility What makes the situation worse is the repeated pattern of closing topics and then reopening or recreating them when they do not receive attention. This creates artificial visibility and keeps the same topics circulating again and again, even when there is no meaningful new information. This turns the issue tracker from a structured bug-reporting system into something closer to a personal complaint board. It also makes it harder for developers and users to distinguish between a genuinely urgent issue and a reposted or duplicated claim. ## Blocking Other Users from Discussion Another serious problem is the use of GitHub’s blocking system. This user appears to be blocking a large number of other community members, which prevents those people from replying to, correcting, or discussing the issues being posted. As a result, the user can publish biased, incorrect, duplicated, or accusatory information while limiting the ability of others to challenge or clarify it. This is unfair to other users and harmful to Valve developers who may rely on issue discussions to understand whether a report is valid. An issue tracker should allow the community to help verify information. If a report contains false claims, missing context, duplicate information, or an incorrect interpretation of game behavior, other users should be able to point that out. When one person can block many of the users who disagree with them and still continue posting large numbers of issues, the process becomes one-sided and unreliable. It creates the appearance of community consensus where none exists, while preventing normal discussion from happening. ## Unofficial Triage and Self-Appointed Confirmation Another concern is that @Dota-Explorer appears to be creating an unofficial parallel triage system inside the repository. They frequently add `#ConfirmedByDEXP` to bugs reported by other users and then include those reports in their own repeatedly created threads. This gives the impression that reports have been formally reviewed, confirmed, or organized through some recognized process, even though this appears to be only the user’s personal label. This is misleading and disruptive. It can make ordinary user comments look like official confirmation, while also redirecting attention from the original reports into @Dota-Explorer’s own threads. In practice, this turns other users’ bug reports into material for a personal tracking system rather than allowing the repository’s normal issue process to work. The issue is not that a user is trying to help confirm bugs. Community confirmation can be useful when done in good faith and without misleading presentation. The problem is the repeated use of a personal confirmation tag, combined with excessive issue creation, reposting, and blocked discussion. Together, this creates a parallel, self-appointed triage process that competes with the actual issue tracker and makes the repository harder to navigate. This also adds to the flooding problem. Instead of keeping discussion focused in the original reports, issues are repeatedly pulled into separate threads, making it harder for Valve developers and other users to follow the original context, reproduction details, and corrections. ## Impact on Developers and Real Bug Reports This behavior has also made the repository much less productive for developers. Instead of receiving clear, focused, reproducible bug reports, users now have to sort through constant noise, repeated claims, personal accusations, and discussions that are intentionally limited by blocking. This wastes time and reduces the chance that real gameplay, WebAPI, and in-game economy issues will be found, confirmed, and fixed. The impact is not theoretical. When serious technical topics such as WebAPI issues or in-game Economics bugs get buried, the entire community loses. ## Why This Is Damaging The current situation is damaging for several reasons: 1. Legitimate bug reports are being buried by excessive issue spam. 2. Important reports, including WebAPI and in-game economy issues, become harder to notice. 3. Duplicate and low-quality reports make the issue tracker harder to search and maintain. 4. Other users are prevented from correcting false or misleading information. 5. Developers receive a distorted view of community feedback. 6. The repository is becoming hostile, unproductive, and increasingly unusable. 7. The issue tracker is being used less like a public bug-reporting tool and more like a personal complaint board. 8. Reopened or recreated issues keep pushing the same topics back to the top without adding useful new information. 9. Unsupported accusations and unverifiable claims create unnecessary conflict and confusion. 10. The normal community process of confirming, reproducing, or disproving bugs is being undermined. ## Clarification I understand that users should be allowed to report bugs frequently, and I do not want to discourage legitimate reports and I completely support the desire to make our favorite game a better place. However, the current pattern appears to go beyond normal participation. The concern is not @Dota-Explorer criticizing the game. The concern is the repeated creation of large numbers of low-quality or duplicate issues, combined with blocking other users who try to correct or discuss them. This should not be allowed to continue. A single user should not be able to dominate the repository, block opposing voices, repeatedly repost closed topics, and present biased or incorrect claims without meaningful community input. ## Possible Solutions ### 1. Add restrictions on how many issues a single user can create per day, week, or month This would probably be the most practical solution. It would not target one specific person unfairly, and it would reduce spam without completely preventing users from reporting bugs. A reasonable limit would force users to prioritize the most important reports instead of opening dozens of issues in a short period of time. It would also help ensure that reports from other users remain visible. This seems especially important because banning one account may not solve the problem. If the user can simply create a new account and continue the same pattern, then broader issue creation limits would be more effective than only account-specific punishment. ### 2. Apply constant moderation to the issue tracker This would help if every low-quality, duplicate, unsupported, or accusatory report could be reviewed and closed quickly. However, this is obviously unrealistic. Developers and maintainers should not have to spend large amounts of time manually cleaning up the issue tracker every day just because one user is flooding it. Moderation can help, but it is not a realistic long-term solution by itself. ### 3. Close down the public Issues section completely This would stop the spam problem, but it would also be very unfortunate for the wider community. The repository has historically been one of the best ways to report real Dota 2 issues directly. Closing Issues entirely would punish everyone because of the behavior of one or a few users. It would also make it harder for legitimate bugs to be reported and tracked publicly. This should probably be considered only as a last resort. ### 4. Ban or limit the specific user This may be necessary if the behavior continues, but a simple ban may not solve the problem completely. The user could simply create a new account and continue the same behavior. Because of that, account-specific action should probably be combined with broader rate limits or moderation rules. Limiting the user’s ability to create new issues may be more effective than only banning the account. ## Recommended Approach Out of these options, the best approach would likely be some combination of issue creation limits and targeted bans for frequent violations. A general rate limit would reduce spam without relying on constant manual cleanup, while specific action could still be taken against accounts that repeatedly abuse the system. This would be more fair to the wider community than closing Issues entirely, and more effective than simply banning one account. ## Closing This repository used to be one of the best resources for reporting and tracking real Dota 2 gameplay problems. Right now, it is becoming increasingly unusable because of one user’s repeated disruptive activity pattern. Important reports are being flooded, technical issues are becoming harder to notice, and normal community discussion is being blocked. This appears inconsistent with the spirit of GitHub’s Acceptable Use Policies, especially the expectation that users should be able to collaborate in good faith without repeated disruption. For the sake of player-to-developers communication, health of the game and the wider player community, this needs to be addressed in a fair, transparent, and constructive way. Thanks in advance for noticing this issue. I sincerely wish this place to be a safe one and, most importantly, a healthy one going long-term. This ambiguity causes players to accidentally delete irreplaceable items. Steps to Reproduce: Own an Arcana with a socketed gem. Purchase a new gem from the Community Market with the intent to swap it. Acquire an Artificer's Chisel. Use the Artificer's Hammer on the Arcana. Observe the confirmation prompt: it asks the player to type "destroy" but does not explicitly state that the Arcana itself will be permanently deleted. Expected Behavior: The confirmation prompt should clearly state: "This action will permanently delete [Item Name]" — if the entire item will be destroyed. "This action will only destroy the extracted gem" — if only the gem is being removed. Players should not be expected to infer which part of the item is being destroyed, especially when dealing with limited-edition, account-bound rewards. Actual Behavior: The current prompt is vague and uses the word "destroy" without specifying the target. Players who are new to the gem extraction mechanic — or who have never used it before — reasonably assume that "destroy" applies to the old gem being removed, not to the Arcana itself. Real Example (Evidence Attached): I am attaching a screenshot from my Steam Inventory History (December 9, 2022) that demonstrates this exact scenario: On Dec 8, I received the Fractal Horns of Inner Abysm (Terrorblade Arcana) from the TI11 Swag Bag. Why This Matters: This bug cost me an account-bound, limited-time TI11 Swag Bag Arcana that is completely irreplaceable. I have no way to re-obtain this item through any in-game or market system. Request: Please review the Artificer's Hammer confirmation prompt to ensure it clearly specifies what is being destroyed (gem vs. base item). Additionally, adding a "Destroyed Item" log entry to the inventory history after a successful Artificer's Hammer use would help players understand what just happened and provide clearer records. Thank you for your time and for considering this feedback. Cosmetic Item Name Fractal Horns of Inner Abysm ### Description The confirmation prompt when using the Artificer's Hammer does not clearly distinguish between destroying an extracted gem and destroying the entire base item (including limited, account-bound Arcanas). This ambiguity causes players to accidentally delete irreplaceable items. Steps to Reproduce: 1 Own an Arcana with a socketed gem. 2 Purchase a new gem from the Community Market with the intent to swap it. 3 Acquire an Artificer's Chisel. 4 Use the Artificer's Hammer on the Arcana. 0 Observe the confirmation prompt: it asks the player to type "destroy" but does not explicitly state that the Arcana itself will be permanently deleted. Expected Behavior: The confirmation prompt should clearly state: "This action will permanently delete [Item Name]" — if the entire item will be destroyed. "This action will only destroy the extracted gem" — if only the gem is being removed. Players should not be expected to infer which part of the item is being destroyed, especially when dealing with limited-edition, account-bound rewards. Actual Behavior: The current prompt is vague and uses the word "destroy" without specifying the target. Players who are new to the gem extraction mechanic — or who have never used it before — reasonably assume that "destroy" applies to the old gem being removed, not to the Arcana itself. Real Example (Evidence Attached): I am attaching a screenshot from my Steam Inventory History (December 9, 2022) that demonstrates this exact scenario: On Dec 8, I received the Fractal Horns of Inner Abysm (Terrorblade Arcana) from the TI11 Swag Bag. On Dec 9, I purchased a new gem (Kinetic: Prosperity Remnants) from the Community Market. I then acquired an Artificer's Chisel and used it on the Arcana. I believed the "destroy" confirmation was for the old gem. Instead, the entire Arcana was deleted. The inventory log does not even show a "Removed" entry — only "Socket added" twice. The item simply vanished without a clear deletion log. This proves the UI failed to communicate what was actually happening. Why This Matters: This bug cost me an account-bound, limited-time TI11 Swag Bag Arcana that is completely irreplaceable. I have no way to re-obtain this item through any in-game or market system. Other Dota 2 players have reported the exact same issue on community forums. Request: Please review the Artificer's Hammer confirmation prompt to ensure it clearly specifies what is being destroyed (gem vs. base item). Additionally, adding a "Destroyed Item" log entry to the inventory history after a successful Artificer's Hammer use would help players understand what just happened and provide clearer records. Thank you for your time and for considering this feedback. ### Example Match ID 12345567 ### Screenshots Dota Team, I am writing to express my growing frustration with the current reporting and Overwatch system in Dota. After approximately 7,000 hours of gameplay, I have experienced and supported the game extensively. It is therefore all the more disappointing for me to see that the current system, in my opinion, is not working fairly. Players are seemingly reported regardless of their actual behavior or their Behavior Score. Reports appear arbitrary and have noticeable negative consequences, even when no wrongdoing has occurred. For example, if you back a buy, even if you overlook the fact that your TP is on cooldown, you get reported, immediately receive a 24-hour Overwatch ban, five SD games, and a 1,000-point score penalty. This development significantly impacts the enjoyment of the game. In its current form, I find the game barely playable, as the system does not adequately differentiate between actual misconduct and unfounded reports. I therefore urge you to fundamentally revise the reporting and Overwatch system. A more transparent, fairer, and more reliable system is urgently needed to sustainably improve the player experience. I've also attended all the TI events. This doesn't just affect me, but many other players as well. Please revise your system so that, for example, three Overwatch reports result in a penalty. This would ensure that toxic players are detected anyway, preventing such misjudgments. Many players blame the replay because they were frustrated by the last match. Another issue is that the lower the behavior score gets, the worse the matchmaking quality becomes. This creates a negative loop where players are pushed into increasingly toxic and unbalanced games, making it even harder to improve their behavior score. A potential solution would be to introduce seasonal rank resets. If ranks were not permanent, boosting services would lose their value, as purchased MMR would not last. This could significantly reduce smurfing and account buying, and help restore fairness to the matchmaking system. At that point, it would be reasonable to evaluate player behavior more strictly, as the gameplay environment itself would be more balanced and fair.
